tags.gist: Strongly supports the paper's direction and calls the clinician training-and-examination model the right instinct for device evaluation.
Wants benchmarking to test sensitivity to who the input claims to come from, their seniority and authority, not only adversarial wording.
Wants the human-oversight dimension tested under realistic override conditions, since a human who can intervene may not.
Wants postmarket monitoring modeled on clinician re-credentialing: periodic re-examination against the original competencies, not drift monitoring alone.
Restates strong support for the paper's direction and the clinician-training analogy.
Restates that benchmarks should test the speaker's claimed identity and authority, since outputs shift with perceived seniority.
Restates that the human-oversight dimension should be tested under realistic override conditions.
Restates the re-credentialing model: periodic re-examination against the original competencies.
Says elements S.2 and R.1 miss one dimension: sensitivity to the claimed identity, seniority and authority of the speaker.
Cites controlled work showing clinical AI outputs shifted more when input was attributed to a senior clinician, without any gain in accuracy.
Argues deference to claimed credentials is a failure mode distinct from adversarial prompting, since the input is an ordinary second opinion.
Suggests R.1 protocols prespecify speaker-authority conditions, with safety behavior that moves with the user's claimed credential counted as failed robustness.
Calls the two axes sound and would add the degree of human oversight as an empirically measured property of the setting, not a present-or-absent feature.
Notes that an override option is often unused under time pressure, and that E.4 treats automation bias only as a communication attribute.
Encourages treating automation bias as a modifier on the activity axis, since unexercised supervision moves a function toward autonomy.
Wants the degree of human oversight demonstrated in representative time-pressured conditions rather than asserted in labeling.
Asks sponsors to show that intended users catch incorrect outputs in realistic workflows, as override-rate and detection-rate evidence.
Says both directiveness and oversight should be judged by observed user behavior, since an unused override interface provides no oversight.
Finds the Section VI approaches reasonable and suggests framing cadence and triggers explicitly as examination-based re-certification.
Proposes re-examining a cleared device on its original competency set on a fixed cycle, plus re-examination after model, prompt or guardrail changes.
Suggests sponsors prespecify the re-examination triggered by any change, rather than every permissible future change.
Would require safety and robustness elements re-run in full after any model or guardrail change, however minor the expected impact.
Would add refusal behavior, content-policy changes between versions and output stability under user framing to master file contents.
Suggests a documented master file let sponsors satisfy parts of re-examination by reference, as an incentive for model developers.
Encourages treating subgroup performance and the anticipated real-world input distribution as one question.
Cites dermatology evidence that shifts in presenting conditions degrade performance more than skin-tone differences alone.
Wants test populations whose disease distribution differs from training data, and sponsors to characterize the expected deployment case mix.
Calls the physician-training analogy the paper's strongest idea and asks FDA to include pressure, hierarchy and unfamiliar patients in the examination.
